title: Overview of Digestive System Physiology and Nutrient Absorption
path: Basic Concepts of Nutrition and Digestion
Overview of Digestive System Physiology and Nutrient Absorption

headings.title: Introduction to the Gastrointestinal Tract and Its Primary Functions
headings.content: The human gastrointestinal tract is a continuous muscular tube running from the mouth to the anus, specialized for transforming consumed food into usable biochemical components. Its primary physiological tasks include ingestion, mechanical and chemical digestion, nutrient absorption, motility, and the elimination of undigested waste. Along this pathway, accessory organs such as the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas secrete vital fluids and enzymes necessary for chemical breakdown. Understanding these foundational processes is essential for midwives, as maternal nutritional status directly depends on how efficiently the digestive tract processes dietary intake.

headings.title: Ingestion, Mastication, and Swallowing Mechanics
headings.content: Digestion begins in the oral cavity through ingestion and mastication, commonly known as chewing. Mastication physically reduces food particle size and mixes food with saliva, which contains the enzyme salivary amylase to initiate carbohydrate breakdown. The resulting softened mass, called a bolus, is then pushed backward by the tongue during the swallowing reflex, also known as deglutition. This process coordinates muscular contractions to safely propel the bolus down the esophagus while the epiglottis closes over the trachea to prevent aspiration.

headings.title: Gastric Secretions and Protein Digestion
headings.content:
Once food enters the stomach, it encounters a highly acidic environment driven by hydrochloric acid, which denatures proteins and kills ingested microorganisms. Specialized cells within the gastric mucosa secrete crucial components:

- **Parietal cells**: Release hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein vital for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
- **Chief cells**: Secrete pepsinogen, an inactive enzyme precursor that converts into active pepsin upon contact with gastric acid.
- **Mucous cells**: Produce a thick bicarbonate-rich mucus layer that shields the stomach lining from self-digestion.

headings.title: Enzymatic Breakdown in the Small Intestine
headings.content: The small intestine is the primary site for chemical digestion and nutrient absorption. As acidic chyme enters the duodenum, it is neutralized by pancreatic bicarbonate. The pancreas also contributes a powerful suite of enzymes, including trypsin, chymotrypsin, pancreatic lipase, and amylase. Simultaneously, the liver produces bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder. Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets, vastly increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase to hydrolyze fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Nutrient Absorption Across the Intestinal Mucosa
headings.content: Nutrient absorption relies heavily on the massive surface area created by circular folds, villi, and microvilli lining the small intestine. Simple sugars and amino acids are transported across the intestinal epithelium into capillary blood via active transport or facilitated diffusion. In contrast, digested fats repackage into water-soluble structures called chylomicrons inside mucosal cells. Because chylomicrons are too large to enter ordinary capillaries, they enter specialized lymphatic vessels called lacteals, eventually reaching the systemic circulation via the thoracic duct.

headings.title: Water and Electrolyte Handling in the Large Intestine
headings.content: By the time digestive contents reach the large intestine, most nutrients have already been absorbed, leaving behind water, electrolytes, and indigestible plant fibers such as cellulose. The colon absorbs significant amounts of water and sodium, transforming liquid chyme into semi-solid feces. Resident gut bacteria also ferment remaining dietary fibers, producing short-chain fatty acids and synthesizing essential micronutrients like vitamin K. Disruptions in large intestine water absorption frequently result in clinical conditions such as diarrhea or constipation.

headings.title: Clinical Implications of Malabsorption in Maternal and Child Nutrition
headings.content: Malabsorption occurs when the gastrointestinal tract fails to adequately absorb nutrients, vitamins, or minerals, posing severe risks during pregnancy and early childhood. In pregnant women, conditions affecting the small intestine can lead to deficiencies in iron, folate, and calcium, predisposing the mother to anemia and bone demineralization. In infants and young children, chronic malabsorption stunts growth, impairs cognitive development, and weakens immune function, contributing significantly to childhood malnutrition. Midwives must recognize early signs of digestive failure, such as chronic diarrhea, poor weight gain, or pallor, to ensure timely nutritional support and medical referral.
